inference-server.name: Inference Server
inference-server.tagline: Async image-classification server with a Redis queue and batched workers
inference-server.summary: A small model-serving system that labels uploaded images with a ResNet18 neural network. A web server accepts each image and hands it to a separate pool of worker processes through a Redis queue. The workers group waiting images into batches, run each batch through the model in one pass, and send every answer back to the request that is waiting for it. Alex built it from scratch as a learning project, along with his own load-testing tool that measures latency and throughput at up to 1,200 simultaneous requests.
inference-server.role: Alex wrote the whole project: all 24 commits from 2026-06-23 to 2026-09-26 are his, 22 under GitHub user ALIUD1 and 2 under a second identity of his, Alex-M-Liu. HANDOFF.md's working rules say main.py (the FastAPI frontend), worker.py (the batching inference worker) and load_test.py (the async load generator) are his own code. He took the design from a single-process FastAPI + ResNet18 endpoint (commit 3f06f73, Jun 24) to separate frontend and worker processes over Redis (2a1cd44, Jul 28). Along the way he added a dedicated reader connection (b876ddd), capped each worker at 1 torch thread (db7a8e1), fixed the reader-task crash (326d74c) and added worker-side batching (c62665e/721acad Aug 14, reworked in b10d04f Sep 26). The read-only diagnostic scripts (diagnose_502.py, inspect_redis.py, single_request.py) and HANDOFF.md were written with AI assistance in a coaching setup, so they should not be credited as his core code.
stack: Redis (lists + key/value; run locally in a Docker Desktop container)
redis-py 8 (redis.asyncio in the frontend, sync client in the workers)

highlights.text: Split the model server into one async FastAPI frontend and N independent worker processes that talk only through Redis. Model inference never runs on the web event loop, and only bytes cross the process boundary.

highlights.text: Matches responses to requests without polling. Each HTTP request waits on an asyncio Future stored under a 16-byte UUID, and one background reader task completes the right Future when its result arrives.

highlights.text: Dynamic batching in the worker: it collects up to 8 queued jobs or waits at most 200 ms, reads all images with one MGET and deletes them with one DEL, then runs a single stacked ResNet18 forward pass under torch.no_grad.

highlights.text: Found why a background task was dying silently. redis-py 8 sets a 5 s default socket timeout, so an unbounded blocking pop failed after 5 s of idle time and killed the reader. Fixed it with a bounded 1 s BLPOP plus a done-callback that prints the task's exception.

highlights.text: Built an asyncio + httpx load generator. It fires 10 to 1,200 concurrent requests per level and reports client and server p25/p50/p75/p95 latency, throughput, and failures grouped by status code.

highlights.text: Spotted survivorship bias in the latency stats: the client's default 5 s timeout was dropping slow requests before they were counted. Raised the read timeout to 30 s so the percentiles include the slow tail.

highlights.text: Capped each worker process at one PyTorch thread so several workers don't fight over the same CPU cores. Gave the blocking response reader its own Redis connection, separate from the request-path pool.

highlights.text: In a committed 4-worker load test (before batching), every request at 10, 100, 200, 300 and 500 concurrent completed with zero failures.

avoid: '31 -> 51 req/s', '1.63x', 'about 1.6x', or the commit message's '1.55 improvement' as a batching speedup. None of these is verified. The 51 req/s table exists only in HANDOFF.md, not in any committed log. The same unbatched 4-worker code ran about 2x faster on Aug 4 than on Aug 12 (server p50 at 10 concurrent was 0.110 s vs 0.214 s). The committed batching log (logs/test.txt) peaks around 23-31 req/s.

Any other number from HANDOFF.md's 'after batching' table: 'p50 cut 26% at peak load', 'saturation moved from ~10 to ~700 concurrent', 'crossover between 300 and 500 concurrent', 'avg batch fill 7.6-7.9 of 8'.
'Worker CPU balanced within 0.2%'. This appears only in HANDOFF.md, and no committed log backs it.

'Batching makes each image 1.47x or 1.58x faster', taken from logs/optimal_batch_test.txt. That microbenchmark ran multi-threaded inside main.py, while the workers run 1 torch thread, where batch 8 saves only about 6-13% per image.
'~31 req/s' as a headline or as the baseline for a speedup. It is a single machine-dependent run (logs/step4_4_workers.txt), and on other days the same code ran much faster.
'Uses LPUSH'. The real ops are SET + RPUSH on 'jobs', BLPOP by the workers, then RPUSH/BLPOP on 'response', which makes both lists FIFO queues.
'Heartbeats', 'failover', 'restarts stalled workers', 'self-healing'. Step 6 was never started, and the repo has no heartbeat code.
'Dockerized' or 'Docker deployment'. There is no Dockerfile; Redis just runs in a local Docker container.
'Model versioning' or 'v1/v2 A/B serving'. This was never built.

'Fault tolerant', 'no lost requests', 'guaranteed delivery'. The frontend awaits the Future with no timeout. If an image fails to decode or a worker dies mid-batch, that request hangs forever, and payload keys have no TTL.
'Horizontally scalable frontend' or 'multiple uvicorn workers'. All frontends share one 'response' list, so a second frontend process would steal the first one's responses.
'Zero failures at 1,200 concurrent'. The committed log shows 147 HTTP 502s at 1,200 concurrent and a few at 700-1000.
'Fixed the 502s' or 'the 502s were caused by a proxy'. The root cause was never confirmed.
'Tuned the batch wait time with a parameter sweep'. The sweep was invalid: load_test.py set worker.BATCH_FILL_WAIT_TIME in its own process, so the running workers never saw the new values.
'GPU inference'. Inference is CPU-only at 1 torch thread per worker.
'Production' or 'serves 1,200 concurrent users'. All of this is a local laptop benchmark.
flow: 1. A client sends HTTP POST / to Uvicorn on port 8001 with an image as multipart form data. The FastAPI handler predict_img reads the bytes from UploadFile and starts a timer.

2. The handler creates a job id with uuid.uuid4().bytes (16 raw bytes). store_coroutine creates an asyncio Future and stores it in the in-memory dict pending_jobs[job_id]. The request is now parked, and the event loop is free to serve other requests.

3. add_to_queue (async redis client, pool max_connections=1000) runs 'SET <job_id> <image_bytes>' to store the payload, then 'RPUSH jobs <job_id>' to put the id at the tail of the 'jobs' list. Only the 16-byte id travels through the queue. The handler then awaits the Future, with no timeout.

4. N separate worker processes (4 in the benchmarks, each with torch.set_num_threads(1)) loop on 'BLPOP jobs 1'. Whichever worker is idle receives the id from the head of the list. If nothing arrives within 1 s it gets None and loops again.

5. The batch window opens on the first job. The worker keeps calling 'BLPOP jobs 0.05' until it holds BATCH_SIZE=8 ids or BATCH_FILL_WAIT_TIME=0.2 s has passed, so a batch closes either when it is full or when the time runs out.
6. The worker fetches every image in one round trip with 'MGET id1..idN', then removes the payload keys with 'DEL id1..idN'.

7. Each image is decoded with Pillow and converted to RGB. ResNet18's default ImageNet transforms (resize 256, center crop 224, normalize) turn it into a [3,224,224] tensor. torch.stack builds a [B,3,224,224] batch and one forward pass under torch.no_grad yields [B,1000] logits. argmax of each row gives that image's ImageNet class index.
8. For each image the worker packs struct.pack('<16sq', job_id, class_idx), a 24-byte message, and runs 'RPUSH response <payload>'.

9. In the frontend, the background task response_reader (started in the FastAPI lifespan, using its own Redis connection r_reader) loops on 'BLPOP response 1' and unpacks each '<16sq' message. awake_coroutine pops the matching Future from pending_jobs and calls set_result(class_idx).
10. The parked handler resumes and returns JSON {"Category_Number": <ImageNet class index>, "Server_Rate": <seconds spent server-side>}. On startup the lifespan also runs FLUSHDB to clear the queues.

inference-server.notes:
Alex, this describes the committed design at HEAD b10d04f. The two uncommitted edits are trivial: main.py adds an unused `import argparse`, and load_test.py deletes the broken `import worker` / `worker.BATCH_FILL_WAIT_TIME = i` sweep lines, so the committed load_test.py still contains the invalid sweep.

Repo hygiene to fix before linking it from a portfolio:
- README.md is UTF-16 and contains only the title.
- The GitHub repo has no description.
- HANDOFF.md is committed and public, and it holds personal coaching and resume notes. Consider removing it from the repo.
- __pycache__/*.pyc files are tracked even though .gitignore excludes them.
- main.py still loads ResNet18 at import time and keeps dead test code in string literals; its `__main__` block calls an undefined test_batching.

Known design limits worth stating honestly:
- The frontend awaits each Future with no timeout.
- A failed image decode, or a batch where every image fails, sends no response, so those requests hang.
- Payload keys have no TTL.
- The single shared 'response' list only works with one frontend process.
- The frontend Redis pool grows to about 1000 connections and never shrinks.

What the committed logs show:
- logs/step4_4_workers.txt (Aug 12, 4 workers, no batching): throughput flat around 31 req/s from 100 to 1000 concurrent, 0 failures through 500, 502s from 700 up (147 at 1,200).
- logs/step4_1_thread_4_workers.txt (Aug 4, same unbatched setup): no throughput line, but latencies were roughly half. This is the evidence for the roughly 2x day-to-day machine variance.
- logs/test.txt (batching, invalid sweep): about 23-31 req/s.
- logs/step5_batching_1_worker.txt and logs/error.txt (1-worker runs): about 11 req/s, collapsing at 700+ concurrent.
- logs/optimal_batch_test.txt: multi-threaded microbenchmark of per-image time at batch sizes 1 to 32.

The memory notes list a controlled interleaved rerun as the planned way to get a defensible batching number. Until that run is committed, describe batching as an architectural feature, not a measured speedup.

For the animation: show 4 worker lanes competing on one FIFO 'jobs' list, a batch tray that closes at 8 items or after 200 ms, and a separate 'response' lane back to one reader that wakes the parked request. Label the Redis ops RPUSH/BLPOP, not LPUSH.

socr-braingen.name: SOCR BrainGen: Atlas-Guided Diffusion for Synthetic Brain MRI
socr-braingen.tagline: Synthetic brain MRI with tumors placed by lobe, generated in ~10 seconds
socr-braingen.summary: In the University of Michigan SOCR lab, Alex built an AI model that generates realistic synthetic brain MRI scans. The user picks where a tumor appears: which brain lobe, how high in the brain, and how large. He trained the model on a public brain-tumor dataset (BraTS 2023) using the university's supercomputer, added it as a sixth model to the lab's existing web app, and deployed it on Hugging Face GPUs, where one scan takes about 10 seconds. He also built the evaluation harness that scores all of the lab's earlier generator models.

flow: 1. CHOOSE: on the website's parameter panel the user picks Tumor (With/Without), Lobe (Frontal, Parietal, Temporal, Occipital, Cerebellum, Insula), Slice location (Inferior/Middle/Superior) and Tumor size (Small/Moderate/Large). On page load the panel asks the Space's conddiff_cells endpoint which lobe x level cells exist (11 of 18) and greys out the rest.

2. REQUEST: the Vercel route /api/generate calls lib/hfSpace.ts. That POSTs {space}/gradio_api/call/generate and gets back an event_id, then GETs the server-sent-event stream until 'event: complete'. The lab's HF token is attached server-side.

3. SEED + SPEC: on the Space, params_to_spec validates the four choices. One random integer seed drives both the mask randomness (numpy) and the starting noise (torch), so every image can be regenerated.

4. PICK ANATOMY: _pick_slice picks a slice at the requested level from the conditioning bank (42 axial slices from 22 held-out BraTS 2023 patients). The chosen lobe must be clearly present: atlas probability > 0.4 over at least 500 px. Output is a 9 x 256 x 256 stack: [FLAIR slot (zeros), T1, mask, 6 lobe probability maps].

5. DRAW THE TUMOR: synth_mask picks a seed pixel inside the lobe, weighted by atlas probability. It sets the target area to a fraction of the lobe's area (small 5-12%, moderate 15-35%, large 40-60%) and scores every pixel as atlas x Gaussian compactness x smoothed random noise. The top-N pixels become the lesion: label 2 is edema, and label 3 is the enhancing core (30% of the lesion). 'Without Tumor' sets the mask to all zeros.
6. BUILD CONDITIONING: build_cond assembles the 8 conditioning channels [T1, tumor mask, 6 lobe maps] as a 1 x 8 x 256 x 256 tensor. It stays constant for the whole loop.
7. START FROM NOISE: x = pure Gaussian noise, 1 x 1 x 256 x 256 (the FLAIR channel), seeded from step 3.

8. DENOISE x200 on the GPU, inside a @spaces.GPU ZeroGPU worker. For t = 995, 990, ..., 5, 0:
- concatenate [x, conditioning] into a 1 x 9 x 256 x 256 input
- the 85.3M-parameter U-Net predicts the noise in x
- the DDIM scheduler removes a calibrated share of it
The image sharpens step by step from static into a brain, with a bright lesion where the mask is.
9. DECODE: map x from [-1, 1] back to [0, 1] and clip, giving the final 256 x 256 synthetic FLAIR slice.
10. ENCODE: to_png_bytes writes the FLAIR PNG in the paper's orientation with fixed 0-1 intensity scaling. If there is a tumor it also writes the mask PNG: edema mid-grey, core white.
11. PUBLISH: the PNGs upload to Supabase storage. The provenance record holds seed, 200 DDIM steps, device=cuda, gpu_seconds (about 6.3 s), source bank slice, and lesion size and coverage.
12. VIEW: the website shows the 'FLAIR' and 'Tumor Mask' tabs. About 10 s pass from click to image.

flow: TSS: NASA's Telemetry Stream Server (SUITS-Techteam TSS) runs on a laptop on the team LAN. It listens on UDP port 14141 and holds rover.json, eva.json, ltv.json and ltv.errors.json.

Poll: the Flask backend (backend/app.py) starts a daemon thread named fetch_loop. For each feed it sends an 8-byte big-endian UDP datagram: [uint32 Unix timestamp][uint32 command]. The commands are 0 for rover, 1 for EVA, 2 for LTV and 3 for LTV errors.
Reply: TSS answers with a single datagram of JSON. udp_client.py decodes the UTF-8 into a Python dict, with a 2 s socket timeout.

Broadcast: the backend stamps local_timestamp and calls socketio.emit('eva-telemetry' / 'rover-telemetry' / 'ltv-telemetry' / 'ltv-errors-telemetry') to every client connected on port 5001. It sleeps 1 s between feeds and 2 s per cycle, so each feed arrives about every 6 s.

Subscribe: there are two listeners. The React SocketProvider uses socket.io-client over a WebSocket, falls back to polling and auto-reconnects. The Unity headset script SocketIOTelemetry.cs subscribes to the same events.
React state: the SocketProvider puts each feed into React state, and useSocket() hands evaData to the /eva page (Alex's code).

Check: the EVA page lays the payload over defaults for EVA-1 and EVA-2, then runs checkRanges(). A value below min or above max gives a red 'danger' alert. A value inside the range but off nominal gives a yellow 'warn' alert. A change |new - prev| / dt above the RATE_LIMITS value gives a 'changing fast' alert. The previous sample and its timestamp are kept in useRef.

Render: alerts are deduped by id and sorted danger-first. Alert ids tint the matching gauge bars, and the alert panel shows the newest 5, merging local alerts with server metric-warnings. The astronaut cards show IMU x, y and heading, and the DCU/UIA switch toggles light up.

Side channels: other clients emit metric-warning (predictive alerts) or matrix-update (a 2D navigation grid). The backend validates and timestamps them, keeps the last 5 warnings and the latest matrix, and rebroadcasts. A client that connects later is sent the cached copies right away.

Command path: a client emits set_throttle 10.0. The backend parses it as a float and sends a 12-byte UDP packet [timestamp][1109][float32] to TSS. TSS replies with 4 bytes, where first byte 0x01 means success. The backend sends udp-command-result to the sender and broadcasts set_throttle-result to everyone.

Onboarding mock: mock_tss.py runs sim_loop 5 times a second. Each step(0.2 s) updates O2 vent/fill, breathing, depress pump, battery and heart rate, checks whether the EVA has started, and moves the astronaut toward the next POI. The full State JSON is then pushed to every /ws WebSocket client.

Onboarding clients: panel.py 'watch' prints one line per frame. Unity TssClient.cs receives frames on a background thread and parks the newest string. Update() on the main thread parses it with JsonUtility, then the EV marker cube lerps to (x, y) and rotates to the heading.

Onboarding control: typing 'uia o2_vent open' in panel.py, or clicking a Unity toggle, sends HTTP POST /uia/o2_vent {"value": true}. The server flips the switch, and on the next tick the O2 tanks start draining for every client. The pytest calls step() directly to fast-forward the whole egress in under a second.

noverwatch.tagline: A Windows service that kills Overwatch the moment it launches.
noverwatch.summary: Noverwatch is a small background program for Windows that Alex built to keep himself off the video game Overwatch. It runs quietly as a Windows service, and the moment Windows reports that Overwatch has started, it shuts the game down and writes the attempt to a log file. Its log shows it closed the game 8 times during testing in March 2026.
noverwatch.role: Solo project. It is not in git, so there are no commits to prove authorship. The evidence is that everything lives under Alex's own Windows profile (C:/Users/alexl/source/repos/Noverwatch), the Visual Studio publish history records 42 publishes between 2026-02-27 and 2026-03-05, and the service 'Noverwatch' is registered on his machine and points at his publish folder. The original work is Noverwatch/Class1.cs, the Detector class, which does all of the following: the WMI process-start watcher, matching the process name against config, recording the PID and timestamp, appending to log.txt, and calling Process.Kill. He also wrote the appsettings.json keys "Games" and "LogPath", the publish setup (self-contained, single-file, ReadyToRun, win-x64), and installed the result as a Windows service. Program.cs and Worker.cs follow the structure of Microsoft's 'Windows Service using BackgroundService' tutorial: AddWindowsService, the EventLog provider registration, and a while loop with Task.Delay. His folder C:/Users/alexl/source/repos/Blocker, dated 2026-02-25, is an unmodified copy of that tutorial's 'Joke Service'. It shows he worked through the tutorial two days before he started Noverwatch on 2026-02-27.

highlights.text: Hypothesis confirmed, with one correction. It does not stop Overwatch from launching. It reacts right after the game process starts and kills it. Detection is event-driven: it subscribes to Windows process-start events with the WMI query "SELECT * FROM Win32_ProcessStartTrace" rather than scanning the process list.

avoid: Saying it 'prevents' or 'blocks' Overwatch from launching. The game process is created first and then killed when the start event arrives.
Saying it 'polls every 100 seconds for Overwatch'. Detection is event-driven through WMI. The 100,000 ms Task.Delay is a heartbeat loop (Worker.cs line 20).
Claiming a kill latency in milliseconds. It was never measured.
Claiming it blocks several games or takes a configurable list. It matches exactly one string, config["Games"].

Claiming it tracks launch-attempt statistics. The in-memory 'blocked' list is never read, and timesBlocked is a local variable inside each detecting() call, so 'Blocked <n>' counts per watcher and is not a lifetime total.

Citing C:/Users/alexl/Noverwatch/logs as the runtime log. It holds only a 12-byte file 'qc' containing the word 'Noverwatch'. The real action log is the repo's Noverwatch/logs/log.txt (the LogPath in appsettings.json).
Saying it runs automatically at boot. The installed service is set to manual start (DEMAND_START) and is currently stopped.
Citing Windows Event Log counts. The 'Noverwatch' and '.NET Noverwatch Service' event sources are registered, but the Application log only goes back to 2026-06-16, so the March events are gone.
Saying it is on GitHub or under version control. There is no .git directory and no remote, and gh is not installed, so a remote check was not possible.
Saying Alex wrote the Windows-service hosting from scratch. Program.cs and Worker.cs follow Microsoft's BackgroundService tutorial (see the Blocker 'Joke Service' copy).
Saying it uses App.config or ConfigurationManager. That line is commented out (Class1.cs line 70); config is read from appsettings.json through IConfiguration.
Saying it kills Battle.net or the whole process tree. Process.Kill() is called without entireProcessTree, so only the matching PID is ended.
Mentioning tests. There are none.
flow: 1. Boot: Windows starts the 'Noverwatch' service (or the developer runs it). Host.CreateApplicationBuilder builds the host, AddWindowsService hooks it into the Service Control Manager, and Detector and Worker are registered through DI.
2. Worker loop, first pass: it logs 'Worker running at: <time>' at Information level, then calls detector.detecting().

3. Arm the tripwire: detecting() creates a ManagementEventWatcher for 'SELECT * FROM Win32_ProcessStartTrace', attaches an EventArrived handler, and calls Start(). This returns immediately, and Windows will now push an event for every new process.
4. Heartbeat: the worker logs the Warning 'The Noverwatch system is online', then sleeps 100 seconds (Task.Delay(100000)). After that it repeats steps 2-4, and each pass adds another watcher.
5. Launch attempt: the user clicks Play and Windows creates Overwatch.exe, for example PID 12400.
6. Detected: WMI fires Win32_ProcessStartTrace and the handler reads ProcessName 'Overwatch.exe' and ProcessID 12400. Every process name, not only Overwatch, is printed to the console.
7. Match check: specificDetector compares 'Overwatch.exe' to config["Games"] ('Overwatch.exe'), ignoring case. Any other process (chrome.exe, etc.) is ignored and the watcher keeps listening.

8. Record: processInfo(12400) looks up the process, adds {Name, pid, DateTime.Now} to an in-memory list, creates the LogPath folder if missing, and appends 'Overwatch PID: 12400 blocked at 3/5/2026 3:53:08 PM' to logs/log.txt.
9. Terminate: killProcess(12400) calls Process.Kill(), the game window disappears, and the Critical log line 'Overwatch has been killed(stopped)! at <time>' is written.
10. Tally: timesBlocked++ is followed by the Critical log 'Blocked 1'. The watcher goes back to listening for the next launch.

Most publishes happened on 2026-03-04 (42 total, 28 succeeded and 14 failed). The first logged kill was 2026-03-04 at 10:16:02 PM. The last source edit (Class1.cs) and the final publish were on 2026-03-05, with the publish at 20:51Z. Seven kills followed on 2026-03-05 between 3:53 and 3:59 PM local time. There has been no activity since.
noverwatch.notes:
The source is 4 small files: Program.cs (21 lines), Worker.cs (33), Class1.cs (113), and config. Line 1 of log.txt holds two entries with no newline between them, the 3/4 one and the first 3/5 one. A likely explanation, which is inference only: the first run used the now commented-out File.WriteAllText (Class1.cs line 48, which writes no newline), and the code then switched to StreamWriter append with WriteLine. These are real code issues worth knowing about if the code is shown publicly, or worth presenting as 'what I'd fix':
(a) Watcher leak. detecting() runs on every 100-second loop pass and creates a new ManagementEventWatcher each time without stopping or disposing the old ones. After N passes there are N handlers on every process start, and they race to log and kill the same PID. GetProcessById sits outside the try block in processInfo, so the later handlers probably throw. That is unverified, but it is consistent with the log never showing a PID twice.
(b) Detection only starts inside `if (logger.IsEnabled(LogLevel.Information))`. If someone raises the log level to Warning, the blocker silently stops working.
(c) `logger.LogError(ex, "Error Message", ex.Message)` has no placeholder for the message it passes.
(d) Process objects are never disposed.
(e) Win32_ProcessStartTrace generally needs admin rights; the service runs as LocalSystem, which satisfies that.
The ServiceName in code ('.NET Noverwatch Service') differs from the installed service name 'Noverwatch'; both event-log sources are registered. Evidence was gathered only with reads plus sc.exe qc, Get-Service, and Get-WinEvent. Nothing was modified. No secrets were found in the project.
